studyMetadata.title: Introducing Mark
studyMetadata.subtitle: Bible Study
studyMetadata.description:
Many people are curious about Jesus. Who was He really? Why did He attract such attention? What made His life so different from anyone else’s? Mark doesn’t begin with background or explanation. It moves straight into the action and lets you see Jesus for yourself.
‘The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.’ (Mark 1:1)
From the outset, Mark makes a bold claim. Jesus is not just a teacher or prophet. He is the Messiah – God’s chosen King – and the Son of God. Everything that follows invites you to watch Him, listen to Him, and decide what you will do with Him.

elements.question: It’s worth reading the whole passage before you begin…
elements.answer:
1The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. 2As it is written in the prophet Isaiah,

“Look, I am sending my messenger ahead of you,
who will prepare your way,
3the voice of one shouting in the wilderness,
‘Prepare the way for the Lord,
make his paths straight.’”

4In the wilderness John the baptizer began preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. 5People from the whole Judean countryside and all of Jerusalem were going out to him, and he was baptizing them in the Jordan River as they confessed their sins. 6John wore a garment made of camel’s hair with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey. 7He proclaimed, “One more powerful than I am is coming after me; I am not worthy to bend down and untie the strap of his sandals. 8I baptize you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”

9Now in those days Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan River. 10And just as Jesus was coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens splitting apart and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. 11And a voice came from heaven: “You are my one dear Son; in you I take great delight.” 12The Spirit immediately drove him into the wilderness. 13He was in the wilderness forty days, enduring temptations from Satan. He was with wild animals, and angels were ministering to his needs.

14Now after John was imprisoned, Jesus went into Galilee and proclaimed the gospel of God. 15He said, “The time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe the gospel!”

elements.text:
Mark wastes no time. There is no birth narrative, no lengthy introduction. From the very first sentence, he tells us exactly who Jesus is — “The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God.” That is the headline. Everything else in the Gospel is the story beneath it.

But as you read on, something surprising emerges. People hear about Jesus. They see what he does. And yet they don’t really understand him. Crowds are amazed. Disciples are confused. Religious leaders are threatened. Even those closest to Jesus misread him again and again. Which raises a question that runs right through Mark’s Gospel — and that these studies will keep bringing us back to: Who is Jesus — and are we seeing him clearly?
The Beginning of the Gospel

elements.passageText:
1The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. 2As it is written in the prophet Isaiah,

“Look, I am sending my messenger ahead of you,
who will prepare your way,
3the voice of one shouting in the wilderness,
‘Prepare the way for the Lord,
make his paths straight.’”

elements.question: What two titles does Mark give Jesus in verse 1, and what does each one claim about him?
elements.questionHint: Look at the words that follow the name ‘Jesus’ in verse 1.
elements.sampleAnswer: Mark calls Jesus ‘Christ’ and ‘the Son of God’. ‘Christ’ is a title, not a surname: it means the Messiah, God’s anointed and long-awaited King. ‘The Son of God’ goes further and claims that Jesus stands in a unique relationship to God himself. Mark puts both titles in his very first sentence, so everything that follows is the story of this person.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God.** Mark gives us the conclusion in the first sentence, then spends the Gospel showing what it means.

elements.text: The word ‘gospel’ simply means ‘good news’, and in Mark’s world it was not a religious word — it was a royal one. When a king won a great victory, or when an heir to the throne was born, heralds went out with the ‘good news’. It was a public announcement of something decisive that had happened. Mark is saying: God is acting. The King is coming. This is not advice for living a better life — it is an announcement that changes everything.

elements.question: Mark calls this the ‘gospel’. How do the words of the prophecy in verses 2–3 show why it is good news?
elements.questionHint: Ask who ‘the Lord’ is in verse 3, and what it means that someone is preparing his way.
elements.sampleAnswer: The prophecy promises a messenger who will prepare the way for ‘the Lord’. The one who comes after the messenger is therefore not just another prophet but the Lord himself. Mark places this prophecy straight after naming Jesus, so he is telling us that in Jesus God has come to his people, as he promised. That is good news because the waiting is over: God has kept his word and acted. It is an announcement of what has happened, not advice about what to do.
elements.mainPoint: **The Lord himself is coming.** The gospel is the announcement that God has kept his promise and arrived in Jesus.

elements.text: Preparing the Way

elements.passageText: 4In the wilderness John the baptizer began preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins. 5People from the whole Judean countryside and all of Jerusalem were going out to him, and he was baptizing them in the Jordan River as they confessed their sins. 6John wore a garment made of camel’s hair with a leather belt around his waist, and he ate locusts and wild honey. 7He proclaimed, “One more powerful than I am is coming after me; I am not worthy to bend down and untie the strap of his sandals. 8I baptize you with water, but he will baptize you with the Holy Spirit.”

elements.question: John says someone more powerful is coming (verses 7–8). Why is repentance the right way to prepare for him?
elements.questionHint: Compare what John’s baptism is ‘for’ in verse 4 with what he says about the one who follows him.
elements.sampleAnswer: John’s baptism is ‘a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins’ (v4). He says the one coming is so much greater than he is that he is not worthy even to untie his sandals, and that he will baptise with the Holy Spirit (v7–8). If someone that great is coming, the right way to meet him is not with self-confidence but with honest acknowledgement of our need. Repentance means turning from our own way, and it prepares us to receive the forgiveness he brings.
elements.mainPoint: **Repentance prepares us to receive the one who forgives.** The greater he is, the more honest we need to be about our need.

elements.text: When a king was about to visit a town, people would prepare — roads were repaired, houses were tidied, officials were put in place. But when John the Baptist prepares the way for Jesus, he doesn’t call people to tidy their towns. He calls them to repent. You don’t prepare for this King by getting your outward life in order. You prepare by honestly facing the inward mess. Repentance is not gloomy — it is the realistic first step toward something wonderful.

elements.question: What did the people do in verse 5, and what might that have cost them?
elements.questionHint: Notice what the people did as well as coming out to John.
elements.sampleAnswer: People from the whole Judean countryside and all of Jerusalem went out to John, were baptised in the Jordan, and confessed their sins (v5). Confessing sins means naming them honestly, not just feeling vaguely imperfect, and doing it in front of others. That would cost them their pride and their reputation, because it admitted that they could not make themselves right with God. The size of the crowd suggests that many people recognised their need and found John’s message compelling rather than merely threatening.
elements.mainPoint: **Repentance is honest, costly confession.** It means admitting real sin, not just a general sense of falling short.

elements.text: The Identity of Jesus Revealed

elements.passageText: 9Now in those days Jesus came from Nazareth in Galilee and was baptized by John in the Jordan River. 10And just as Jesus was coming up out of the water, he saw the heavens splitting apart and the Spirit descending on him like a dove. 11And a voice came from heaven: “You are my one dear Son; in you I take great delight.”

elements.question: What happens as Jesus comes up out of the water in verses 10–11, and what does it tell us about who he is?
elements.questionHint: Make a list of the three things that happen, and who is involved in each.
elements.sampleAnswer: The heavens split apart, the Spirit descends on Jesus like a dove, and a voice from heaven speaks (v10–11). The splitting heavens show God breaking into the moment, and the Spirit marks Jesus out as the one God has empowered for his mission. The voice of the Father declares, ‘You are my one dear Son; in you I take great delight.’ So Jesus is not merely a prophet or a teacher but God’s own Son, in whom the Father delights. Father, Son and Spirit are all present at this moment.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus is God’s own Son.** At his baptism the Father speaks, the Spirit descends and the Son stands in the water.

elements.text: Before Jesus has preached a single sermon or performed a single miracle, God speaks. “You are my one dear Son; in you I take great delight.” This is striking. Usually we think of identity as something we earn — through achievement, through reputation, through what others think of us. But here, Jesus’ identity is declared before anything he has done publicly. He is the beloved Son. That is the foundation, not the conclusion.

elements.question: The voice speaks before Jesus has preached or healed anyone. What does that timing tell us?
elements.questionHint: Look at what Mark has and has not told us Jesus has done by verse 11.
elements.sampleAnswer: Mark has told us nothing yet of Jesus’ teaching or miracles, so the Father’s words cannot be a reward for achievement. Jesus’ identity as the beloved Son is given, not earned. His ministry begins from the Father’s delight in him rather than working towards it. The same pattern is true for those who belong to Christ: acceptance comes first, and service flows from it.
elements.mainPoint: **Identity comes before performance.** The Father’s delight in the Son is declared before Jesus has done anything.

elements.text: Tested but Faithful

elements.passageText: 12The Spirit immediately drove him into the wilderness. 13He was in the wilderness forty days, enduring temptations from Satan. He was with wild animals, and angels were ministering to his needs.

elements.question: What does verse 12 say about how Jesus came to be in the wilderness, and what does that suggest?
elements.questionHint: Notice who acts in verse 12, the verb Mark uses and the word ‘immediately’.
elements.sampleAnswer: The Spirit, who has just come down on Jesus, ‘immediately drove him into the wilderness’. Jesus does not wander there by accident; it is part of God’s purpose for him. Mark gives no gentle easing into ministry — straight after the Father’s affirmation comes direct confrontation. The Spirit’s strong action shows that facing temptation was part of the mission Jesus came to fulfil.
elements.mainPoint: **The Spirit sends Jesus into the testing.** Temptation is part of his mission, not an accident.

elements.text: Immediately after his baptism, Jesus is driven into the wilderness. He is tested. Mark doesn’t give us the details that Matthew and Luke do, but the point is clear: where human beings have failed again and again — where Israel failed, where Adam failed — Jesus stands firm. This matters enormously. His faithfulness is not a footnote; it is part of what makes him the Saviour we need.

elements.question: What does verse 13 tell us about the opposition Jesus faces and the help he receives?
elements.questionHint: Look at who is against him and who is with him in verse 13.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus faces direct opposition from Satan himself for forty days, and he is in a dangerous place among wild animals. Yet he is not left alone: angels are ministering to his needs. Mark does not give the details of the temptations, but he makes clear that Jesus endures them. His mission begins with a battle against evil, and he comes through it sustained by God. The forty days recall Israel’s forty years in the wilderness, where Israel failed and Jesus does not.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus stands firm where others fell.** He is tested by Satan, and God sustains him through it.

elements.text: The Message of the Kingdom

elements.passageText: 14Now after John was imprisoned, Jesus went into Galilee and proclaimed the gospel of God. 15He said, “The time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe the gospel!”

elements.question: What two things does Jesus announce at the start of verse 15, and what do they mean together?
elements.questionHint: Notice that ‘fulfilled’ looks back, while ‘near’ describes something now arriving.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus says, ‘The time is fulfilled and the kingdom of God is near.’ The ‘time’ is the long period of waiting and promise in the Old Testament, and he says it is now complete. The ‘kingdom of God’ is God’s own rule, and it has drawn near in the person of Jesus himself. Together the two statements mean that the moment God promised has arrived. This is good news announced before it is a command given.
elements.mainPoint: **God’s long-promised rule has arrived in Jesus.** The time is fulfilled and the kingdom is near.

elements.text: “Repent and believe the gospel!” That is Jesus’ summary of his own message. It has two parts, and they belong together. Repentance without faith is just guilt. Faith without repentance is just wishful thinking. Together, they describe a complete turning — away from one way of living, and toward the King who has arrived. The kingdom of God is not a distant hope. It has come near. In Jesus, it has arrived.

elements.question: Jesus gives two commands in verse 15. What are they, and why do they belong together?
elements.questionHint: Ask what each command would be like if you tried to do it without the other.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus commands, ‘Repent and believe the gospel!’ To repent is to turn away from our own way of living, and to believe is to trust that the good news about Jesus is true and to stake our lives on it. Repentance without faith leaves only guilt and regret, with nowhere to turn. Faith without repentance is claiming to trust Jesus while carrying on in the same direction. Together they describe a complete turning towards the King who has arrived.
elements.mainPoint: **Turn and trust.** Repentance turns us from the old way; faith turns us to the King.

elements.text: Reflection Questions

elements.question: What assumptions do you bring about who Jesus is? Where have they come from?
If repentance and faith go together at the start of the Christian life, how are you doing at living out both of them today?
What would it mean for you — practically and specifically — to respond to Jesus as King this week?

elements.text: Prayer Focus

Ask God to help you see Jesus clearly, not through the filter of your expectations, but as Mark presents him. Confess any areas where you have been resisting what he calls you to. Ask for the faith to trust him, and the courage to follow.
Application Challenge
Each morning this week, begin the day with this short prayer: “Jesus, you are King — help me to follow you today.” Notice what it brings up. Notice where it feels costly.

elements.answer:
16As he went along the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew, Simon’s brother, casting a net into the sea (for they were fishermen). 17Jesus said to them, “Follow me, and I will turn you into fishers of people!” 18They left their nets immediately and followed him. 19Going on a little farther, he saw James, the son of Zebedee, and John his brother in their boat mending nets. 20Immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and followed him.

21Then they went to Capernaum. When the Sabbath came, Jesus went into the synagogue and began to teach. 22The people there were amazed by his teaching, because he taught them like one who had authority, not like the experts in the law. 23Just then there was a man in their synagogue with an unclean spirit, and he cried out, 24“Leave us alone, Jesus the Nazarene! Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God!” 25But Jesus rebuked him: “Silence! Come out of him!” 26After throwing him into convulsions, the unclean spirit cried out with a loud voice and came out of him. 27They were all amazed so that they asked each other, “What is this? A new teaching with authority! He even commands the unclean spirits and they obey him.” 28So the news about him spread quickly throughout all the region around Galilee.

29Now as soon as they left the synagogue, they entered Simon and Andrew’s house, with James and John. 30Simon’s mother-in-law was lying down, sick with a fever, so they spoke to Jesus at once about her. 31He came and raised her up by gently taking her hand. Then the fever left her and she began to serve them. 32When it was evening, after sunset, they brought to him all who were sick and demon-possessed. 33The whole town gathered by the door. 34So he healed many who were sick with various diseases and drove out many demons. But he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him.

35Then Jesus got up early in the morning when it was still very dark, departed, and went out to a deserted place, and there he spent time in prayer. 36Simon and his companions searched for him. 37When they found him, they said, “Everyone is looking for you.” 38He replied, “Let us go elsewhere, into the surrounding villages, so that I can preach there too. For that is what I came out here to do.” 39So he went into all of Galilee preaching in their synagogues and casting out demons.

40Now a leper came to him and fell to his knees, asking for help. “If you are willing, you can make me clean,” he said. 41Moved with indignation, Jesus stretched out his hand and touched him, saying, “I am willing. Be clean!” 42The leprosy left him at once, and he was clean. 43Immediately Jesus sent the man away with a very strong warning. 44He told him, “See that you do not say anything to anyone, but go, show yourself to a priest, and bring the offering that Moses commanded for your cleansing, as a testimony to them.” 45But as the man went out he began to announce it publicly and spread the story widely, so that Jesus was no longer able to enter any town openly but stayed outside in remote places. Still they kept coming to him from everywhere.

2:1Now after some days, when he returned to Capernaum, the news spread that he was at home. 2So many gathered that there was no longer any room, not even by the door, and he preached the word to them. 3Some people came bringing to him a paralytic, carried by four of them. 4When they were not able to bring him in because of the crowd, they removed the roof above Jesus. Then, after tearing it out, they lowered the stretcher the paralytic was lying on. 5When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” 6Now some of the experts in the law were sitting there, turning these things over in their minds: 7“Why does this man speak this way? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?” 8Now immediately, when Jesus realized in his spirit that they were contemplating such thoughts, he said to them, “Why are you thinking such things in your hearts? 9Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Stand up, take your stretcher, and walk’? 10But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,”—he said to the paralytic — 11“I tell you, stand up, take your stretcher, and go home.” 12And immediately the man stood up, took his stretcher, and went out in front of them all. They were all amazed and glorified God, saying, “We have never seen anything like this!”

elements.text:
There is a difference between being impressed by someone and being willing to submit to them. You might be impressed by a surgeon’s skill without trusting her with your own operation. You might admire a great leader without following his instructions. Amazement and submission are not the same thing.

In this section of Mark, people are constantly amazed by Jesus. But amazement is not the same as understanding — and understanding is not the same as obedience. As we look at Jesus’ authority in teaching, in action, and over sin itself, the question to keep asking is not “Is Jesus impressive?” but “Am I submitted to him?”
The Call to Follow

elements.passageText: 16As he went along the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew, Simon’s brother, casting a net into the sea (for they were fishermen). 17Jesus said to them, “Follow me, and I will turn you into fishers of people!” 18They left their nets immediately and followed him. 19Going on a little farther, he saw James, the son of Zebedee, and John his brother in their boat mending nets. 20Immediately he called them, and they left their father Zebedee in the boat with the hired men and followed him.

elements.question: How do the four fishermen respond when Jesus calls them, and what does Mark’s wording stress?
elements.questionHint: Look for the word Mark uses in verses 18 and 20.
elements.sampleAnswer: Simon, Andrew, James and John all follow Jesus without delay. Mark stresses this with the word ‘immediately’: they ‘left their nets immediately’ (v18), and James and John go as soon as Jesus calls them (v20). There is no negotiation, no request for time to think and no conditions. Mark wants us to feel the weight of Jesus’ call: it carries such authority that the right response is simply to follow.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus’ call is met with immediate obedience.** His authority leaves no room for delay.

elements.text: Jesus says two words: “Follow me.” And they follow. Immediately. They leave nets, boats, and — in the case of James and John — their father. No negotiation, no questions, no conditions. This is not presented as reckless impulsiveness. It is presented as the right response to Jesus. His call is immediate and costly, and the right answer is to go.

elements.question: What do the four men leave behind in verses 18 and 20, and what does Jesus offer them in verse 17?
elements.questionHint: Compare the things they leave with the one thing Jesus says he will make them.
elements.sampleAnswer: Simon and Andrew leave their nets, which were their livelihood, and James and John leave their father Zebedee and the hired men in the boat. They give up work, security and family ties. Jesus offers them himself — ‘Follow me’ — and a new purpose: ‘I will turn you into fishers of people!’ He is not merely asking for their time but promising to reshape who they are and what their lives are for.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus asks for everything, and gives himself and a new purpose.** He calls them to follow him and promises to make them fishers of people.

elements.text: Authority in Teaching and Power

elements.passageText:
21Then they went to Capernaum. When the Sabbath came, Jesus went into the synagogue and began to teach. 22The people there were amazed by his teaching, because he taught them like one who had authority, not like the experts in the law. 23Just then there was a man in their synagogue with an unclean spirit, and he cried out, 24“Leave us alone, Jesus the Nazarene! Have you come to destroy us? I know who you are—the Holy One of God!” 25But Jesus rebuked him: “Silence! Come out of him!” 26After throwing him into convulsions, the unclean spirit cried out with a loud voice and came out of him. 27They were all amazed so that they asked each other, “What is this? A new teaching with authority! He even commands the unclean spirits and they obey him.” 28So the news about him spread quickly throughout all the region around Galilee.

29Now as soon as they left the synagogue, they entered Simon and Andrew’s house, with James and John. 30Simon’s mother-in-law was lying down, sick with a fever, so they spoke to Jesus at once about her. 31He came and raised her up by gently taking her hand. Then the fever left her and she began to serve them. 32When it was evening, after sunset, they brought to him all who were sick and demon-possessed. 33The whole town gathered by the door. 34So he healed many who were sick with various diseases and drove out many demons. But he would not permit the demons to speak, because they knew him.

elements.question: How does the crowd describe Jesus’ teaching in verses 22 and 27, and what connects it to his command over the unclean spirit?
elements.questionHint: Look for the word ‘authority’ in both verses.
elements.sampleAnswer: In verse 22 the people are amazed because Jesus taught ‘like one who had authority, not like the experts in the law’. In verse 27, after he silences the unclean spirit and it comes out, they exclaim, ‘A new teaching with authority! He even commands the unclean spirits and they obey him.’ The crowd links what he says with what he does: the same authority is at work in his words and in his commands. His teaching is not only information, because it carries the power to make evil obey.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus’ authority is seen in both his words and his actions.** The same word of command teaches the crowd and drives out evil.

elements.text: Jesus teaches in the synagogue, and the crowd is astonished — not at the content, but at the authority. He doesn’t say, “Rabbi So-and-so argues that…” He simply speaks, and what he says carries weight. Then he acts: he commands an unclean spirit and it obeys. He heals the sick. Word spreads across the whole region. His authority is not limited to the lecture hall — it extends over the spiritual realm and the physical body. It is absolute and it is real.

elements.question: How does Mark show that Jesus’ authority is real and not just claimed (verses 23–34)?
elements.questionHint: List who or what responds to Jesus, from the synagogue to the door of the house in the evening.
elements.sampleAnswer: In the synagogue the unclean spirit obeys his command and comes out (v25–26). At Simon’s house the fever leaves Simon’s mother-in-law at his touch, and she gets up and serves them (v30–31). By evening the whole town gathers, and Jesus heals many who are sick and drives out many demons (v32–34). Even the demons know him as ‘the Holy One of God’ (v24), and he will not let them speak (v34). His authority covers evil spirits, illness and crowds alike, and it is effective wherever he uses it.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus’ authority is demonstrated, not merely claimed.** Spirits, sickness and crowds all respond to him.

elements.text: Authority to Forgive

elements.passageText: 1Now after some days, when he returned to Capernaum, the news spread that he was at home. 2So many gathered that there was no longer any room, not even by the door, and he preached the word to them. 3Some people came bringing to him a paralytic, carried by four of them. 4When they were not able to bring him in because of the crowd, they removed the roof above Jesus. Then, after tearing it out, they lowered the stretcher the paralytic was lying on. 5When Jesus saw their faith, he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” 6Now some of the experts in the law were sitting there, turning these things over in their minds: 7“Why does this man speak this way? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?” 8Now immediately, when Jesus realized in his spirit that they were contemplating such thoughts, he said to them, “Why are you thinking such things in your hearts? 9Which is easier, to say to the paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Stand up, take your stretcher, and walk’? 10But so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,”—he said to the paralytic — 11“I tell you, stand up, take your stretcher, and go home.” 12And immediately the man stood up, took his stretcher, and went out in front of them all. They were all amazed and glorified God, saying, “We have never seen anything like this!”

elements.question: What does Jesus see in verse 5, and what do the four men do to show it?
elements.questionHint: Look at what Jesus responds to before he says anything to the paralysed man.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus sees their faith. The men cannot get through the crowd, so they dig through the roof above Jesus and lower the paralysed man on his stretcher (v4). Their faith is shown by what they do: they let nothing stand in the way of bringing their friend to Jesus. It is in response to that faith that Jesus speaks to the man.
elements.mainPoint: **Faith acts.** The friends’ determined effort to bring the man to Jesus is what Jesus sees.

elements.question: Why do the experts in the law object to Jesus’ words in verse 5, and are they right about forgiveness?
elements.questionHint: Read their question at the end of verse 7 and ask what it assumes about who can forgive sins.
elements.sampleAnswer: The experts in the law think Jesus is blaspheming, because he has told the man, ‘Your sins are forgiven’ (v5, 7). Their question, ‘Who can forgive sins but God alone?’, is correct: forgiveness belongs to God. So by saying it, Jesus is either claiming to be God or committing blasphemy. They cannot accept the first possibility, so they assume the second. Their error is not about forgiveness but about who Jesus is.
elements.mainPoint: **Only God can forgive sins.** The experts in the law are right about that, which is why Jesus’ claim is so startling.

elements.text: When a paralysed man is lowered through a roof by his friends, Jesus doesn’t say what anyone expects. He says, “Son, your sins are forgiven.” The experts in the law are immediately on alert. They are right to be: forgiving sins is something only God can do. Jesus is not making a modest claim. Either he is blaspheming, or he is exactly who he is implying he is. He then heals the man to demonstrate that his authority to forgive is real. This is the hinge moment of this section. Jesus doesn’t just have authority over sickness and evil — he has authority over sin itself.

elements.question: What does Jesus say in verse 10 that he wants them to know, and how does the healing support it?
elements.questionHint: Look at the words ‘so that you may know’ in verse 10.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus wants them to know that ‘the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins’. That is a claim to the authority that belongs to God. He asks which is easier, to say ‘Your sins are forgiven’ or to say ‘Stand up, take your stretcher, and walk’ (v9). No one can see whether the first has happened, but when the man stands up and walks out, the second proves the first. The healing is the visible evidence of Jesus’ invisible authority.
elements.mainPoint: **The healing proves Jesus’ authority to forgive.** The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.

elements.text: Reflection Questions

elements.question: There is a difference between finding Jesus impressive and being genuinely submitted to him. Which best describes where you are right now?
Jesus calls people to follow him completely, not to admire him from a distance. What might hold you back, or what are you holding back from his authority?
The paralysed man’s friends went to extraordinary lengths to bring him to Jesus. Is there someone in your life you could be doing more to bring to him?

elements.text: Application Challenge

elements.text:
It is tempting to assume that the people who opposed Jesus were obviously wicked, while those who followed him clearly saw the truth. But Mark’s account is more uncomfortable than that. The opposition to Jesus in these chapters does not come from the obviously irreligious. It comes from the religious — from people who loved God’s law, who attended the synagogue, who cared deeply about right and wrong. And they couldn’t see Jesus for who he was.

This raises an unsettling question: is it possible to be deeply religious and still be blind to what God is actually doing?
Wrong Expectations

elements.question: What does Jesus do in verses 14–15 that the experts in the law and the Pharisees object to, and how does he answer them in verse 17?
elements.questionHint: Jesus’ answer is a short saying about a doctor.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus calls Levi, a tax collector, to follow him, and then shares a meal with many tax collectors and sinners in Levi’s home (v14–15). Eating together meant fellowship and acceptance, so the experts in the law and the Pharisees object (v16). Jesus replies that those who are healthy do not need a physician, but those who are sick do, and that he has ‘not come to call the righteous, but sinners’ (v17). He is not breaking God’s heart for people but fulfilling it, by going to those who know they need help.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus came for sinners.** He eats with those who know they are sick because they are the ones who need a physician.

elements.text: Jesus sits down to eat with tax collectors and sinners. This is not a small thing in his culture. To eat with someone was to honour them, to declare fellowship with them. The Pharisees are scandalised. But Jesus is not violating God’s law — he is fulfilling God’s heart. The problem is that they have a clear picture of what a godly man should look like, and Jesus doesn’t match it. Their expectations have become a wall between them and the truth.

elements.question: In verses 21–22 Jesus uses two pictures, a patch and wineskins. What goes wrong in each, and what is he saying about what he has brought?
elements.questionHint: Ask what happens when something new is forced together with something old.
elements.sampleAnswer: If someone sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment, the patch pulls away and the tear becomes worse. If new wine is poured into old wineskins, the wine bursts the skins and both are destroyed. Jesus is saying that what he brings is genuinely new and cannot be fitted into the old religious framework the Pharisees were trying to keep. New wine needs new wineskins, and trying to contain him in old categories will only tear and burst them.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus brings something new that old frameworks cannot contain.** Forcing him into familiar categories only tears and bursts them.

elements.text: Hard Hearts

elements.passageText: 1Then Jesus entered the synagogue again, and a man was there who had a withered hand. 2They watched Jesus closely to see if he would heal him on the Sabbath, so that they could accuse him. 3So he said to the man who had the withered hand, “Stand up among all these people.” 4Then he said to them, “Is it lawful to do good on the Sabbath, or evil, to save a life or destroy it?” But they were silent. 5After looking around at them in anger, grieved by the hardness of their hearts, he said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” He stretched it out, and his hand was restored. 6So the Pharisees went out immediately and began plotting with the Herodians, as to how they could assassinate him.

elements.question: What are the people in the synagogue watching for in verse 2, and what do they do after the healing in verse 6?
elements.questionHint: Compare what they are looking for in verse 2 with how they respond in verse 6.
elements.sampleAnswer: They watch Jesus closely to see whether he will heal on the Sabbath, ‘so that they could accuse him’ (v2). When he asks whether it is lawful to do good or evil on the Sabbath, to save a life or destroy it, they are silent (v4). After the man’s hand is restored, the Pharisees go out immediately and begin plotting with the Herodians about how to assassinate Jesus (v6). They came looking for a charge, not for God, and even an act of healing cannot move them.
elements.mainPoint: **Hard hearts can watch a miracle and plot a murder.** The Pharisees came for evidence against Jesus, not for God.

elements.text: A man with a withered hand is there. Jesus heals him. And in response — to an act of compassion and restoration — the Pharisees immediately begin plotting to kill Jesus. Mark records that Jesus looks around at them ‘in anger, grieved by the hardness of their hearts’. This is not a clash of opinion about theology. This is what spiritual blindness looks like at its worst: watching a miracle happen and responding with murderous intent. Hard hearts can watch God at work and see only a threat.

elements.question: What does Mark say Jesus feels in verse 5, and what does that show about what is wrong with the people watching him?
elements.questionHint: Notice the two feelings Mark names, and what they are directed at.
elements.sampleAnswer: Mark says Jesus looked round at them ‘in anger, grieved by the hardness of their hearts’. His anger and grief are not about their opinions but about their hearts. They have refused to answer his question about doing good and saving life, and they would rather keep their rules and plans than see a man restored. A hard heart is one that can watch grace at work and feel nothing but threat. Jesus’ anger is a grieved anger, not a loss of temper.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus is angry and grieved at hardness of heart.** Their problem is not their theology but their unwillingness to rejoice in what God is doing.

31Then Jesus’ mother and his brothers came. Standing outside, they sent word to him, to summon him. 32A crowd was sitting around him and they said to him, “Look, your mother and your brothers are outside looking for you.” 33He answered them and said, “Who are my mother and my brothers?” 34And looking at those who were sitting around him in a circle, he said, “Here are my mother and my brothers! 35For whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother.”

elements.question: What two different explanations are given for Jesus’ behaviour in verses 21 and 22, and who gives them?
elements.questionHint: One comes from his family and the other from experts who ‘came down from Jerusalem’.
elements.sampleAnswer: His family go out to restrain him because they say, ‘He is out of his mind’ (v21). The experts in the law who came down from Jerusalem say, ‘He is possessed by Beelzebul’, and that he casts out demons ‘by the ruler of demons’ (v22). Both groups see the same remarkable activity and cannot accept it for what it is. The family treat it as madness; the experts treat it as demonic. Neither group has a category for who Jesus really is.
elements.mainPoint: **Even Jesus’ family and the religious experts misread him.** Neither can fit him into a category they already have.

elements.question: How does Jesus answer the charge that he is working by Satan’s power (verses 23–27)?
elements.questionHint: Follow his two pictures: a divided kingdom or house, and a strong man’s house.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus points out that Satan cannot cast out Satan: a kingdom or house divided against itself cannot stand (v23–26). If Satan were fighting himself, his end would have come. Instead Jesus uses the picture of a strong man’s house, which cannot be plundered unless the strong man is first tied up (v27). The implication is that Jesus is the stronger one, overpowering Satan and freeing his captives. What the experts call demonic is in fact the defeat of Satan.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus is the stronger one who plunders Satan’s house.** His power over demons shows Satan is being defeated, not served.

elements.text: By this point, even Jesus’ family thinks he has lost his mind. The experts in the law from Jerusalem conclude he is empowered by the devil. Not strangers — his own family and the nation’s religious scholars. It would be easy to dismiss these people as foolish or malicious. But Mark seems to want us to feel the weight of it: if even those closest to him misunderstood him this badly, how confident should we be that we are seeing him clearly?

elements.question: How does Jesus describe his true family in verses 33–35, and what does that suggest about belonging to him?
elements.questionHint: Compare who is standing outside with who is sitting around Jesus in a circle.
elements.sampleAnswer: When his mother and brothers send word from outside, Jesus asks, ‘Who are my mother and my brothers?’ He looks at those sitting around him and says, ‘Here are my mother and my brothers!’ He then says that ‘whoever does the will of God is my brother and sister and mother’ (v35). Belonging to Jesus is not a matter of blood, closeness or religious learning but of doing God’s will. Those who are submitted to God are in a position to recognise who Jesus is.
elements.mainPoint: **True belonging is doing the will of God.** Closeness or learning is not enough; Jesus’ family are those who submit to God.

elements.text: Reflection Questions

elements.question: The religious leaders were sincere people who thought they were serving God — and yet they missed him completely. Does that concern you? Why or why not?
Are there ways you have constructed a picture of Jesus that is more comfortable than the real thing? How can religion itself become a way of resisting him?
“True belonging”, Jesus says, means doing the will of God (3:35). How does that challenge the way you think about your relationship with him?

elements.text: Application Challenge
Take a piece of paper and write down the question: “Where am I resisting Jesus — and why?” Sit with it honestly. Don’t rush to a comfortable answer. Then bring what you have written to him in prayer.

10When he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. 11He said to them, “The secret of the kingdom of God has been given to you. But to those outside, everything is in parables,

12so that although they look they may look but not see,
and although they hear they may hear but not understand,
so they may not repent and be forgiven.”

13He said to them, “Don’t you understand this parable? Then how will you understand any parable? 14The sower sows the word. 15These are the ones on the path where the word is sown: Whenever they hear, immediately Satan comes and snatches the word that was sown in them. 16These are the ones sown on rocky ground: As soon as they hear the word, they receive it with joy. 17But they have no root in themselves and do not endure. Then, when trouble or persecution comes because of the word, immediately they fall away. 18Others are the ones sown among thorns: They are those who hear the word, 19but worldly cares, the seductiveness of wealth, and the desire for other things come in and choke the word, and it produces nothing. 20But these are the ones sown on good soil: They hear the word and receive it and bear fruit, one thirty times as much, one sixty, and one a hundred.”

21He also said to them, “A lamp isn’t brought to be put under a basket or under a bed, is it? Isn’t it to be placed on a lampstand? 22For nothing is hidden except to be revealed, and nothing concealed except to be brought to light. 23If anyone has ears to hear, he had better listen!” 24And he said to them, “Take care about what you hear. The measure you use will be the measure you receive, and more will be added to you. 25For whoever has will be given more, but whoever does not have, even what he has will be taken from him.”

26He also said, “The kingdom of God is like someone who spreads seed on the ground. 27He goes to sleep and gets up, night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he does not know how. 28By itself the soil produces a crop, first the stalk, then the head, then the full grain in the head. 29And when the grain is ripe, he sends in the sickle because the harvest has come.”

30He also asked, “To what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable can we use to present it? 31It is like a mustard seed that when sown in the ground, even though it is the smallest of all the seeds in the ground— 32when it is sown, it grows up, becomes the greatest of all garden plants, and grows large branches so that the wild birds can nest in its shade.”

33So with many parables like these, he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear. 34He did not speak to them without a parable. But privately he explained everything to his own disciples.

elements.text:
Have you ever read a passage of the Bible many times and suddenly, one day, it means something entirely different to you — not because the words changed, but because you did? That experience points to something Jesus teaches directly in this chapter. The problem with understanding God’s word is not usually a problem with the word. It is a problem with the listener.

Jesus teaches large crowds in parables — vivid, earthy stories drawn from everyday life. And he does this, he says, so that those outside “may look but not see” and “may hear but not understand.” This is challenging. Jesus is not saying his teaching is unclear. He is saying that the condition of the heart determines whether the message gets through.
The Parable of the Sower

elements.question: In Jesus’ explanation, what stops the word from bearing fruit in the first three soils (verses 15–19)?
elements.questionHint: Make a list of the obstacle in each soil, and notice which are dramatic and which are quiet.
elements.sampleAnswer: On the path, Satan comes immediately and snatches the word away (v15). On the rocky ground, people receive the word with joy but have no root, so when trouble or persecution comes because of the word they fall away (v16–17). Among the thorns, ‘worldly cares, the seductiveness of wealth, and the desire for other things’ come in and choke the word so that it produces nothing (v18–19). Only the last of these involves no dramatic opposition: it is simply the slow crowding out of the word by ordinary concerns.
elements.mainPoint: **The same seed meets three different obstacles.** Satan snatches it, pressure withers it and the cares of life choke it.

elements.text: A farmer scatters seed on four kinds of ground. The seed is the same in every case — the same word, the same message. What differs is the soil. Some seed is snatched away before it takes root. Some springs up quickly but has no depth and withers. Some grows but is choked out by competing concerns. And some falls on good soil and produces an extraordinary harvest. Jesus is not describing four different kinds of people out there. He is holding up a mirror.

elements.question: What marks the good soil in verse 20, and how does it differ from the other three?
elements.questionHint: Look at what the good soil does with the word, and what the result is.
elements.sampleAnswer: The good soil hears the word, receives it and bears fruit — ‘one thirty times as much, one sixty, and one a hundred’ (v20). The other soils may hear and even receive, but the word is snatched away, withers or is choked, so nothing lasts. The mark of good soil is not just hearing but a hearing that lasts and produces fruit. The fruit comes in varying amounts, but it is real.
elements.mainPoint: **Good soil hears, receives and bears fruit.** The difference is not the seed but how the word is received.

elements.text: Why Parables?

elements.passageText:
10When he was alone, those around him with the twelve asked him about the parables. 11He said to them, “The secret of the kingdom of God has been given to you. But to those outside, everything is in parables,

12so that although they look they may look but not see,
and although they hear they may hear but not understand,
so they may not repent and be forgiven.”

elements.question: What do the people in verse 10 do when they do not understand, and what does Jesus give them in verse 11?
elements.questionHint: Notice when and how they ask, and who is with them.
elements.sampleAnswer: When Jesus is alone, those around him with the twelve ask him about the parables (v10). They do not assume they already understand, and they do not walk away with the surface story. Jesus tells them, ‘The secret of the kingdom of God has been given to you’ (v11). By contrast, to those outside everything is in parables. Those who press in and ask are given understanding.
elements.mainPoint: **Those who ask are given the secret of the kingdom.** The disciples press in rather than walking away.

elements.text: When the disciples ask Jesus privately about the parables, he gives a striking answer. The parables are not simply illustrations to make things clearer — they are a kind of test. Those who are genuinely open and seeking come closer; those who are closed find the story lands lightly and passes on. This is not cruelty on Jesus’ part. It is a description of how spiritual perception works. A person who is genuinely hungry for truth will press in. A person who is satisfied with their current understanding will not.

elements.question: Verse 12 speaks of people who ‘look but not see’ and ‘hear but not understand’. What does this suggest about the kind of listener who does grasp the parables?
elements.questionHint: Contrast those described in verse 12 with those who ask in verse 10.
elements.sampleAnswer: Verse 12 describes people who look and hear but get no further than the surface, so that they do not repent and are not forgiven. The disciples in verse 10 are different: they are hungry to understand, so they ask. The parables reveal the condition of the listener as much as they reveal the truth about the kingdom. Someone who is satisfied with their current understanding will stay on the surface, while someone who presses in will be given more.
elements.mainPoint: **The parables test the listener’s heart.** Those who press in receive understanding; those who stay satisfied stay on the surface.

elements.text: The Growing Kingdom

elements.passageText:
26He also said, “The kingdom of God is like someone who spreads seed on the ground. 27He goes to sleep and gets up, night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows, though he does not know how. 28By itself the soil produces a crop, first the stalk, then the head, then the full grain in the head. 29And when the grain is ripe, he sends in the sickle because the harvest has come.”

30He also asked, “To what can we compare the kingdom of God, or what parable can we use to present it? 31It is like a mustard seed that when sown in the ground, even though it is the smallest of all the seeds in the ground— 32when it is sown, it grows up, becomes the greatest of all garden plants, and grows large branches so that the wild birds can nest in its shade.”

33So with many parables like these, he spoke the word to them, as they were able to hear. 34He did not speak to them without a parable. But privately he explained everything to his own disciples.

elements.question: In the parable of the growing seed (verses 26–29), who does the work of growth?
elements.questionHint: Notice what the man does, what happens while he sleeps, and what the soil does ‘by itself’.
elements.sampleAnswer: The man spreads the seed, then goes to sleep and gets up, night and day, while the seed sprouts and grows ‘though he does not know how’ (v27). The soil produces a crop by itself, first the stalk, then the head, then the full grain (v28). When the grain is ripe he sends in the sickle because the harvest has come. The growth is not produced by his understanding or effort. The kingdom grows by God’s own power.
elements.mainPoint: **The kingdom grows by God’s power, not ours.** The farmer sows and reaps, but the growth in between is not his doing.

elements.text: The farmer scatters seed — and then goes to sleep. He doesn’t understand how growth happens. He simply trusts that it will. The seed does its work in the dark. And the result — a harvest from a tiny beginning — is out of all proportion to what seemed possible at the start. This is how God’s kingdom works. It is not always visible. It does not always feel dramatic. But it is growing.

elements.question: In the mustard seed parable (verses 30–32), what contrast does Jesus draw, and what does it say about the kingdom?
elements.questionHint: Compare how the seed begins with what it becomes.
elements.sampleAnswer: The mustard seed is ‘the smallest of all the seeds in the ground’, yet when sown it grows up and becomes ‘the greatest of all garden plants’, with branches large enough for wild birds to nest in its shade (v31–32). The contrast is between a tiny beginning and a huge result. The kingdom may begin small and unimpressive, as it did with a teacher in Galilee, but its end will be out of all proportion to its start.
elements.mainPoint: **Small beginnings, great end.** The kingdom may look insignificant now, but it will be out of all proportion to its start.

elements.text: Reflection Questions

35On that day, when evening came, Jesus said to his disciples, “Let’s go across to the other side of the lake.” 36So after leaving the crowd, they took him along, just as he was, in the boat, and other boats were with him. 37Now a great windstorm developed and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was nearly swamped. 38But he was in the stern, sleeping on a cushion. They woke him up and said to him, “Teacher, don’t you care that we are about to die?” 39So he got up and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Be quiet! Calm down!” Then the wind stopped, and it was dead calm. 40And he said to them, “Why are you cowardly? Do you still not have faith?” 41They were overwhelmed by fear and said to one another, “Who then is this? Even the wind and sea obey him!”

5:1So they came to the other side of the lake, to the region of the Gerasenes. 2Just as Jesus was getting out of the boat, a man with an unclean spirit came from the tombs and met him. 3He lived among the tombs, and no one could bind him anymore, not even with a chain. 4For his hands and feet had often been bound with chains and shackles, but he had torn the chains apart and broken the shackles in pieces. No one was strong enough to subdue him. 5Each night and every day among the tombs and in the mountains, he would cry out and cut himself with stones. 6When he saw Jesus from a distance, he ran and bowed down before him. 7Then he cried out with a loud voice, “Leave me alone, Jesus, Son of the Most High God! I implore you by God —do not torment me!” 8(For Jesus had said to him, “Come out of that man, you unclean spirit!”) 9Jesus asked him, “What is your name?” And he said, “My name is Legion, for we are many.” 10He begged Jesus repeatedly not to send them out of the region. 11There on the hillside, a great herd of pigs was feeding. 12And the demonic spirits begged him, “Send us into the pigs. Let us enter them.” 13Jesus gave them permission. So the unclean spirits came out and went into the pigs. Then the herd rushed down the steep slope into the lake, and about 2,000 were drowned in the lake.

14Now the herdsmen ran off and spread the news in the town and countryside, and the people went out to see what had happened. 15They came to Jesus and saw the demon-possessed man sitting there, clothed and in his right mind—the one who had the “Legion”—and they were afraid. 16Those who had seen what had happened to the demon-possessed man reported it, and they also told about the pigs. 17Then they began to beg Jesus to leave their region. 18As he was getting into the boat the man who had been demon-possessed asked if he could go with him. 19But Jesus did not permit him to do so. Instead, he said to him, “Go to your home and to your people and tell them what the Lord has done for you, that he had mercy on you.” 20So he went away and began to proclaim in the Decapolis what Jesus had done for him, and all were amazed.

21When Jesus had crossed again in a boat to the other side, a large crowd gathered around him, and he was by the sea. 22Then one of the synagogue leaders, named Jairus, came up, and when he saw Jesus, he fell at his feet. 23He asked him urgently, “My little daughter is near death. Come and lay your hands on her so that she may be healed and live.” 24Jesus went with him, and a large crowd followed and pressed around him.

25Now a woman was there who had been suffering from a hemorrhage for twelve years. 26She had endured a great deal under the care of many doctors and had spent all that she had. Yet instead of getting better, she grew worse. 27When she heard about Jesus, she came up behind him in the crowd and touched his cloak, 28for she kept saying, “If only I touch his clothes, I will be healed.” 29At once the bleeding stopped, and she felt in her body that she was healed of her disease. 30Jesus knew at once that power had gone out from him. He turned around in the crowd and said, “Who touched my clothes?” 31His disciples said to him, “You see the crowd pressing against you and you say, ‘Who touched me?’” 32But he looked around to see who had done it. 33Then the woman, with fear and trembling, knowing what had happened to her, came and fell down before him and told him the whole truth. 34He said to her, “Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace, and be healed of your disease.”

35While he was still speaking, people came from the synagogue leader’s house saying, “Your daughter has died. Why trouble the teacher any longer?” 36But Jesus, paying no attention to what was said, told the synagogue leader, “Do not be afraid; just believe.” 37He did not let anyone follow him except Peter, James, and John, the brother of James. 38They came to the house of the synagogue leader where he saw noisy confusion and people weeping and wailing loudly. 39When he entered he said to them, “Why are you distressed and weeping? The child is not dead but asleep!” 40And they began making fun of him. But he forced them all outside, and he took the child’s father and mother and his own companions and went into the room where the child was. 41Then, gently taking the child by the hand, he said to her, “Talitha koum,” which means, “Little girl, I say to you, get up.” 42The girl got up at once and began to walk around (she was twelve years old). They were completely astonished at this. 43He strictly ordered that no one should know about this, and told them to give her something to eat.

6:1Now Jesus left that place and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. 2When the Sabbath came, he began to teach in the synagogue. Many who heard him were astonished, saying, “Where did he get these ideas? And what is this wisdom that has been given to him? What are these miracles that are done through his hands? 3Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? And aren’t his sisters here with us?” And so they took offense at him. 4Then Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown, and among his relatives, and in his own house.” 5He was not able to do a miracle there, except to lay his hands on a few sick people and heal them. 6And he was amazed because of their unbelief. Then he went around among the villages and taught.

elements.text:
Suppose someone you trusted promised to take care of you — and then, the very next day, something frightening happened. Would you trust the promise, or would the fear take over? Most of us know the answer from experience. When fear is immediate and the promise feels distant, fear usually wins. That is exactly what happens to the disciples in this section of Mark. They have seen Jesus at work. They have heard him teach. And when a storm hits the boat, they panic.

Jesus’ response is not primarily a lesson about weather. It is a question aimed straight at the heart: “Do you still not have faith?”
Fear vs Faith

elements.passageText: 35On that day, when evening came, Jesus said to his disciples, “Let’s go across to the other side of the lake.” 36So after leaving the crowd, they took him along, just as he was, in the boat, and other boats were with him. 37Now a great windstorm developed and the waves were breaking into the boat, so that the boat was nearly swamped. 38But he was in the stern, sleeping on a cushion. They woke him up and said to him, “Teacher, don’t you care that we are about to die?” 39So he got up and rebuked the wind, and said to the sea, “Be quiet! Calm down!” Then the wind stopped, and it was dead calm. 40And he said to them, “Why are you cowardly? Do you still not have faith?” 41They were overwhelmed by fear and said to one another, “Who then is this? Even the wind and sea obey him!”

elements.question: How does Jesus respond to the disciples’ fear in verse 40, and what does that show he expected of them?
elements.questionHint: Notice that Jesus asks two questions instead of offering comfort.
elements.sampleAnswer: After calming the wind and sea with a word, Jesus turns to the disciples and asks, ‘Why are you cowardly? Do you still not have faith?’ (v40). The word ‘still’ implies that they should by now have learned to trust him. He is not surprised that the storm was frightening, but he expected their confidence in him to hold. Fear had pushed out trust.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus expects trust, even in a storm.** His question is aimed at their faith, not at the weather.

elements.text: The storm is real. The danger is real. The disciples’ fear is entirely understandable. What is striking is that Jesus is asleep in the stern — not oblivious, but at rest. When they wake him in a panic, he calms the storm with a word and then turns to them with a question. Not “Are you all right?” but “Why are you cowardly? Do you still not have faith?” The implication is that they had everything they needed to trust him — they just didn’t.

elements.question: How do the disciples react after the storm is calmed (verse 41), and what question are they left with?
elements.questionHint: Compare their fear in verse 38 with their fear in verse 41.
elements.sampleAnswer: In verse 38 they feared the storm, but in verse 41 they are ‘overwhelmed by fear’ at what Jesus has done. They ask each other, ‘Who then is this? Even the wind and sea obey him!’ They have seen his power but have not yet grasped who he is. Mark leaves the question hanging for the reader, because it is the question the whole Gospel is answering.
elements.mainPoint: **The disciples see the power but not yet the person.** ‘Who then is this?’ is the question Mark wants us to keep asking.

elements.question: How does the man’s reaction to Jesus in verses 6–13 show who has authority?
elements.questionHint: Compare what no one could do to the man in verses 3–4 with what Jesus does in verse 8.
elements.sampleAnswer: No one could bind the man, not even with a chain, and no one was strong enough to subdue him (v3–4). Yet when he sees Jesus he runs and bows down before him, and he calls him ‘Son of the Most High God’ (v6–7). Jesus commands the spirit to come out and asks its name, and the spirits beg to be sent into the pigs and go only when Jesus gives them permission (v8–13). Every move the spirits make is under Jesus’ control, so he is stronger than a force no human could contain.
keyTerms: son of the most high god|most high
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus has complete authority over evil.** A force no human could restrain bows to him and begs his permission.

elements.text: Jesus confronts a man so tormented by evil that no chains could hold him — and delivers him completely. But notice that not everyone who sees it is glad. The people who come out to find out what has happened are afraid. Seeing power is not the same as trusting the one who holds it.

elements.question: How do the local people respond to Jesus in verses 15–17, and what does Jesus tell the healed man to do instead (verse 19)?
elements.questionHint: Compare what the crowd asks Jesus to do in verse 17 with what Jesus asks the man to do in verse 19.
elements.sampleAnswer: The people see the man sitting there, clothed and in his right mind, and they are afraid; they then beg Jesus to leave their region (v15–17). They have seen undeniable power, but it frightens them and does not lead to faith. The healed man wants to go with Jesus, but Jesus tells him to go home and tell his people ‘what the Lord has done for you, that he had mercy on you’ (v19). He does so, proclaiming in the Decapolis what Jesus had done for him, and all are amazed (v20).
elements.mainPoint: **Seeing Jesus’ power does not guarantee faith.** The crowd begs him to leave, while the healed man is sent to tell of God’s mercy.

elements.question: What did the woman’s faith look like in verses 25–28, and what does Jesus say about it in verse 34?
elements.questionHint: Notice what she had already tried, what she kept saying and what she did.
elements.sampleAnswer: The woman had suffered from bleeding for twelve years, had endured the care of many doctors, had spent all she had, and had only got worse (v25–26). When she heard about Jesus she came up behind him in the crowd and touched his cloak, because she kept saying, ‘If only I touch his clothes, I will be healed’ (v27–28). Her faith was a desperate, personal trust that Jesus could do what no one else had. Jesus tells her, ‘Daughter, your faith has made you well. Go in peace’ (v34).
elements.mainPoint: **Faith is desperate trust in Jesus.** The woman had exhausted every other remedy and came to him.

elements.text: In a single chapter, Jesus delivers a man no one could restrain. He heals a woman who had been suffering for twelve years and had exhausted every human remedy. And he is about to raise a twelve-year-old girl from death. These are not three random miracles. They are a comprehensive demonstration. There is no darkness Jesus cannot enter. There is no suffering beyond his reach. There is no door, including death’s, that he cannot open.

elements.question: When the news comes that the girl has died (verse 35), what does Jesus tell Jairus to do, and what happens?
elements.questionHint: Compare what the messengers say in verse 35 with what Jesus says in verse 36.
elements.sampleAnswer: People from the synagogue leader’s house say, ‘Your daughter has died. Why trouble the teacher any longer?’ (v35). Jesus pays no attention to what was said and tells Jairus, ‘Do not be afraid; just believe’ (v36). At the house he takes the girl by the hand and says, ‘Little girl, I say to you, get up’, and she gets up at once and walks around (v41–42). Jesus’ authority reaches even to death, and he calls Jairus to keep trusting him when the situation seems beyond help.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus has authority even over death.** He calls Jairus to ‘just believe’ when all seems lost.

elements.text: Familiarity Breeds Unbelief

elements.passageText: 1Now Jesus left that place and came to his hometown, and his disciples followed him. 2When the Sabbath came, he began to teach in the synagogue. Many who heard him were astonished, saying, “Where did he get these ideas? And what is this wisdom that has been given to him? What are these miracles that are done through his hands? 3Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? And aren’t his sisters here with us?” And so they took offense at him. 4Then Jesus said to them, “A prophet is not without honor except in his hometown, and among his relatives, and in his own house.” 5He was not able to do a miracle there, except to lay his hands on a few sick people and heal them. 6And he was amazed because of their unbelief. Then he went around among the villages and taught.

elements.question: What do the people of Nazareth say about Jesus in verses 2–3, and how do they respond to him?
elements.questionHint: Notice what astonishes them and what they use to dismiss him.
elements.sampleAnswer: Many who hear him in the synagogue are astonished and ask where he got his wisdom and how these miracles are done through his hands (v2). But then they say, ‘Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary…?’, and name his brothers and ask about his sisters (v3). They cannot get past what they already know about him, and ‘so they took offense at him’. Their familiarity with his background becomes the reason they reject him.
elements.mainPoint: **Familiarity can become a barrier to faith.** The people of Nazareth are astonished, yet reject Jesus because they think they already know him.

elements.text: Jesus returns to Nazareth. These are people who have known him since childhood — watched him grow up, worked alongside his family. And precisely because they think they know him, they cannot receive him. “Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary…?” They are so sure they have him figured out that they cannot see who he really is. Mark notes something remarkable: Jesus ‘was not able to do a miracle there’, except to heal a few sick people — not because his power was limited, but because their unbelief shut the door.

elements.question: What do verses 5–6 say about the effect of the people’s unbelief?
elements.questionHint: Look at what Jesus was not able to do, and how he felt about it.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus ‘was not able to do a miracle there, except to lay his hands on a few sick people and heal them’ (v5). Mark adds that ‘he was amazed because of their unbelief’ (v6). Unbelief does not reduce Jesus’ power, but it closes the door to receiving what he would do. Jesus then goes on teaching in the surrounding villages.
elements.mainPoint: **Unbelief shuts the door on what Jesus would do.** Jesus himself is amazed at it.

elements.text: Reflection Questions

elements.question: What fears, right now, are competing with your faith? Have you brought them honestly to Jesus, or have you been trying to manage them yourself?
Jesus’ hometown knew him — and missed him. Is there a danger that you have become so used to Jesus that you have stopped really seeing him?
If Jesus has authority over evil, suffering and death, what does that mean for the specific situation you are facing right now?

elements.text: Application Challenge

Identify one specific fear that is weighing on you this week. Each day, bring it to Jesus in prayer — not just mentioning it, but deliberately placing it in his hands. Notice whether anything changes, not in the circumstances, but in you.

27Then Jesus and his disciples went to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that I am?” 28They said, “John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and still others, one of the prophets.” 29He asked them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered him, “You are the Christ.” 30Then he warned them not to tell anyone about him.

31Then Jesus began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and experts in the law, and be killed, and after three days rise again. 32He spoke openly about this. So Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. 33But after turning and looking at his disciples, he rebuked Peter and said, “Get behind me, Satan. You are not setting your mind on God’s interests, but on man’s.”

34Then Jesus called the crowd, along with his disciples, and said to them, “If anyone wants to become my follower, he must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. 35For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life because of me and because of the gospel will save it. 36For what benefit is it for a person to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his life? 37What can a person give in exchange for his life? 38For if anyone is ashamed of me and my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.” 9:1And he said to them, “I tell you the truth, there are some standing here who will not experience death before they see the kingdom of God come with power.”

elements.text:
Every story has a hinge — a moment when everything turns. In Mark’s Gospel, that moment is here. Jesus and his disciples are walking through the villages near Caesarea Philippi, and Jesus asks them two questions. The first is warm-up: “Who do people say that I am?” The second is the one that counts: “But who do you say that I am?”

That second question does not stay safely in the first century. It comes forward through the pages of the Gospel and lands directly in front of every reader. You cannot stay neutral on it. The question demands an answer.
Who Do You Say I Am?

elements.passageText: 27Then Jesus and his disciples went to the villages of Caesarea Philippi. On the way he asked his disciples, “Who do people say that I am?” 28They said, “John the Baptist, others say Elijah, and still others, one of the prophets.” 29He asked them, “But who do you say that I am?” Peter answered him, “You are the Christ.” 30Then he warned them not to tell anyone about him.

elements.question: What two questions does Jesus ask in verses 27 and 29, and how do the answers differ?
elements.questionHint: Compare what the disciples report in verse 28 with Peter’s reply in verse 29.
elements.sampleAnswer: First Jesus asks, ‘Who do people say that I am?’, and the disciples report that others say John the Baptist, Elijah or one of the prophets (v27–28). Then he asks, ‘But who do you say that I am?’ (v29). The first question asks what other people think; the second demands a personal answer from the disciples themselves. Peter answers, ‘You are the Christ’, which goes beyond the opinions of the crowd. Jesus will not let the disciples hide behind what other people say.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus presses the personal question: ‘Who do you say that I am?’** Borrowed opinions are not enough.

elements.text: Peter answers immediately and correctly: “You are the Christ.” It is the right answer. It is the answer the whole Gospel has been building toward. But as the very next section shows, getting the title right is not the same as understanding what it means. Peter knows who Jesus is — but he is about to show that he has badly misunderstood why Jesus has come.

elements.question: Peter answers, ‘You are the Christ.’ How would you answer Jesus’ question in your own words?
elements.questionHint: Try to say what you believe about Jesus, beyond repeating a title.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus is the Christ — the promised Messiah, God’s appointed King, who came not to conquer by force but to rescue his people through his death and resurrection. He is fully human, born into history, and yet the one in whom God’s own authority and identity are present. He has the right to call me to follow him, and my only real hope rests in him. He is not only a teacher or a moral example; he is the living Lord to whom I owe my whole life.
elements.mainPoint: **Jesus is the Christ, the living Lord.** A faithful answer says who he is and what he has done, and submits to him.

elements.text: A Shocking Mission

elements.passageText: 31Then Jesus began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and experts in the law, and be killed, and after three days rise again. 32He spoke openly about this. So Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him. 33But after turning and looking at his disciples, he rebuked Peter and said, “Get behind me, Satan. You are not setting your mind on God’s interests, but on man’s.”

elements.question: What does Jesus teach about himself in verse 31, and how does Peter respond in verse 32?
elements.questionHint: List what the Son of Man ‘must’ go through, and who rejects him.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus teaches that the Son of Man ‘must suffer many things’ and be rejected by the elders, chief priests and experts in the law, be killed, and after three days rise again (v31). He speaks openly about it (v32). Peter takes him aside and begins to rebuke him. Peter has just called Jesus the Christ, and a Messiah who suffers, is rejected and is killed does not fit what he expected. He assumes that God’s chosen king should win, not be handed over to his enemies.
elements.mainPoint: **The Christ must suffer, be killed and rise.** Peter’s rebuke shows how unexpected that is.

elements.text: Jesus begins to explain what being the Christ actually involves: rejection, suffering, death, and then resurrection. Peter cannot accept it. He takes Jesus aside and rebukes him. This is not a small moment of doubt — it is a direct challenge to Jesus’ understanding of his own mission. And Jesus’ response is fierce: “Get behind me, Satan.” Peter has got the identity right but the mission completely wrong. He is imagining a Messiah shaped by human hopes — a conqueror, not a servant; a throne, not a cross.

elements.question: What does Jesus say is wrong with Peter’s thinking in verse 33?
elements.questionHint: Notice the contrast between ‘God’s interests’ and ‘man’s’.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus rebukes Peter and says, ‘You are not setting your mind on God’s interests, but on man’s’ (v33). Peter assumes that God works through strength and success, and that a true king would not suffer defeat. Jesus calls him ‘Satan’ because, in trying to steer Jesus away from the cross, Peter is opposing God’s plan. The cross inverts human expectations: God’s greatest work is done through what looks like total defeat.
elements.mainPoint: **Peter’s mind is on man’s interests, not God’s.** God’s way to victory runs through the cross.

elements.text: The Call to Discipleship

elements.passageText: 34Then Jesus called the crowd, along with his disciples, and said to them, “If anyone wants to become my follower, he must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me. 35For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life because of me and because of the gospel will save it. 36For what benefit is it for a person to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his life? 37What can a person give in exchange for his life? 38For if anyone is ashamed of me and my words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when he comes in the glory of his Father with the holy angels.”

elements.question: Jesus says that anyone who wants to follow him must ‘deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me’ (verse 34). What does that involve, given what he has just said about his own path in verse 31?
elements.questionHint: Link verse 34 with what Jesus said in verse 31 about what ‘must’ happen to him.
elements.sampleAnswer: Jesus has just described his own path of rejection, suffering and death in verse 31, and he now calls his followers to follow him on that road. A cross was an instrument of execution, so taking up a cross means walking towards death and giving up any claim to run your own life. To ‘deny himself’ means that my agenda, comfort, reputation and even safety are no longer the supreme concern. The specific cost will differ for each person, but the call is the same.
elements.mainPoint: **Following Jesus means taking his road of the cross.** It is a call to lay down the right to run your own life.

elements.text: Having spoken about his own path of suffering, Jesus turns to the crowd and explains what following him involves. “If anyone wants to become my follower, he must deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” This is not an invitation to a comfortable life with Jesus as a helpful addition. It is a call to reorient your entire existence around him — to stop living for yourself, and to start living for him, whatever the cost.
